problem_statement: The paper frames the task as pricing European-style Asian FX options, specifically Asian currency options whose payoff depends on the average exchange rate over a period. It says these contracts are used for hedging currency-linked cash-flow risk, but are hard to price because there is no closed-form pricing formula.
problem_statement_quotes: FX options are derivative instruments used to manage currency-linked risks.
An important class of FX options is Asian options, which are contracts with payoffs depending on the average exchange rate over some time period.
The main drawback of these contracts is that they are usually hard to price. There is no closed-form pricing formula
classical_baseline: The paper treats classical Monte Carlo simulation as the main baseline for valuing these options, while also mentioning other classical numerical approaches such as distribution approximations, lattice methods, and PDE methods. It explicitly says classical Monte Carlo is still very often used for valuing these contracts.
classical_baseline_quotes: the classical Monte Carlo algorithms are still very often used for valuing these contracts.
One of such methods is Monte Carlo simulation which was introduced by Boyle in [5].
A different class of algorithms used for pricing Asian options are lattice methods, which are modifications of the binomial Cox, Ross and Rubinstein model described in [8].
classical_difficulty: The paper says Monte Carlo accuracy improves only like the inverse square root of the number of samples, so achieving good precision requires many simulated paths and is time consuming. It also says this can be expensive and slow in practice, especially for institutions pricing large numbers of instruments.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Hence we conclude that the accuracy of the estimate shrinks like the inverse square root of the number of samples and it is proportional to the standard deviation of H(S).

The former is the largest drawback of the Monte Carlo methods, as the satisfying precision of the estimate involves generating a large amount of simulated price paths, which is usually time consuming.

Classical Monte Carlo algorithm is widely used in pricing derivatives, but in many advanced instruments it is required to make a huge amount of simulation to get a price with acceptable error. In practice, it may turn out to be an expensive and slow method especially for institutions that have to price large amounts of instruments.
business_stakes: The paper says these options are used by corporate treasurers to hedge regular cash flows, and that pricing matters in practice because institutions may need to price large amounts of instruments. It also notes that the local volatility model is important because volatility smile is usually observed on financial markets.
business_stakes_quotes: Such instruments are commonly used by corporate treasurers, as they are often lower priced and better suited for hedging risk related to cash flows exchanged on a regular basis.
In practice, it may turn out to be an expensive and slow method especially for institutions that have to price large amounts of instruments.

This is a very important fact from the practical point of view because the volatility smile is usually observed on the financial markets and the local volatility model is one of the most important in the practical pricing of financial derivatives.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in abstract and introduction; paper is a pricing-method paper with clear classical Monte Carlo baseline.
